records.name: Samsun
records.current_summary: No province-specific measure, incident or institution concerning transgender visitors is documented here in this edition's audited sources: what governs a trans visitor is the national picture, and no local authority is recorded adding bans or enforcement programs of its own.  The national framework as documented: a draft judicial package leaked in October 2025 would carry terms up to three years for conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, up to four for same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies, raise the gender-care age floor to twenty-five with mandatory infertility conditions, and remove civil-status recognition of gender change. The principal national LGBTI report (Feb 2026) called the previous year's hostility explicit state policy — 'Year of the Family' directives, censorship instructions, one organisation closed, three hate-motivated killings with trans victims over-represented, 89 ill-treatment cases mostly tied to breaking up gatherings, and 313 detentions.  Samsun is the Black Sea's largest urban centre. Absence of provincial documentation describes the record, not a guarantee: national directives reach every province's institutions, and the assembly-ban and violence patterns were logged countrywide rather than per province.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch news release (29 Oct 2025): the leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' (up to 3 years; participation in same-sex ceremonies up to 4 years), raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 with mandatory infertility and multi-evaluation hurdles, and imprison providers (up to 7 years) and patients (up to 3 years); fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association object.

Wikipedia's 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page, the national framework that governs Samsun (a Black Sea province where national law applies): homosexuality has been decriminalised in Turkey since 1858, and sex-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, but legal gender recognition still requires a court's permission under Civil Code Article 40 with the applicant at least 18, unmarried and holding a medical report from a state-designated hospital. The Turkish military bars homosexuals from service and treats homosexuality as a 'psychosexual' illness, and Istanbul Pride drew roughly 100,000 participants in 2013-2014 before the 2015-2018 parades were banned by local authorities. No province-specific rule for Samsun is recorded here; the provisions above apply nationwide, including to Samsun's residents and visitors.

Amnesty International's November 2025 factsheet analyses the leaked '11th Judicial Package', a 66-page draft amending the Turkish Penal Code, Civil Code and six other laws that was leaked to Turkish media in mid-October 2025. It is the third set of proposed legal amendments targeting LGBTI+ rights in 2025, the earlier two having stalled in Parliament. The draft would raise the minimum age for legal gender recognition procedures from 18 to 25 and add further conditions; Amnesty warns it would criminalise LGBTI+ people and those advocating for their rights, and would severely restrict or make impossible trans and gender-diverse people's access to gender-affirming healthcare. These are nationwide proposals that would apply within every province including Samsun, whose record already notes the leaked October 2025 package.

Amnesty's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26) records the national framework governing a visitor to Siirt: in June 2025 blanket bans were issued against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, over 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. The report also records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public in 2025 — criminalizing LGBTI identity expression and consensual same-sex relations and making legal gender recognition nearly impossible — though they were ultimately not submitted to parliament. No Siirt-specific incident is documented; this is the province-level applicable national framework.

records.current_summary: No province-specific measure, incident or institution concerning transgender visitors is documented here in this edition's audited sources: what governs a trans visitor is the national picture, and no local authority is recorded adding bans or enforcement programs of its own.  The national framework as documented: a draft judicial package leaked in October 2025 would carry terms up to three years for conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality, up to four for same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies, raise the gender-care age floor to twenty-five with mandatory infertility conditions, and remove civil-status recognition of gender change. The principal national LGBTI report (Feb 2026) called the previous year's hostility explicit state policy — 'Year of the Family' directives, censorship instructions, one organisation closed, three hate-motivated killings with trans victims over-represented, 89 ill-treatment cases mostly tied to breaking up gatherings, and 313 detentions.  Sivas is a central Anatolian interior province. Absence of provincial documentation describes the record, not a guarantee: national directives reach every province's institutions, and the assembly-ban and violence patterns were logged countrywide rather than per province.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch news release (29 Oct 2025): the leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' (up to 3 years; participation in same-sex ceremonies up to 4 years), raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 with mandatory infertility and multi-evaluation hurdles, and imprison providers (up to 7 years) and patients (up to 3 years); fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association object.

Wikipedia's national 'LGBT rights in Turkey' page is the framework every Turkish province, Sivas included, stands under: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 (with sex reassignment surgery, medical examination and court permission), but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from serving in the Turkish military: a health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and the resulting 'unfit report' can leak and fuel later discrimination in public life. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised, and when the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 the anti-LGBTQ provisions were removed from the bill, leaving only symbolic same-sex weddings possible. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against participants who defied the bans. The page also records early-2026 press reports that the government considered legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', and that Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking.

Amnesty International's Türkiye country report (Report 2025/26): in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans pride marches in Istanbul, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, while prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. For this record it evidences the national enforcement climate - blanket bans plus case-by-case prosecutions under the same Law No. 2911 - that applies to provincial authorities in Sivas just as it does across Turkey.

records.name: Tokat
records.current_summary: No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation exists for this province. That absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence — not as evidence of local permissiveness: the nationwide framework below governs here as in every province.  As documented nationally: a judicial package leaked in October 2025 would make conduct judged contrary to biological sex or general morality punishable by up to three years, criminalise same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to four years), and bar gender-affirming care under age 25 behind a permanent-infertility assessment, with patients and providers exposed to prosecution; civil-society groups and the country's medical association protested, and an established human-rights court precedent is invoked against it. The 2025 report of the country's longest-running LGBTI monitoring body describes hostility becoming explicit state policy — 'family' directives to public institutions, the first closure of an LGBTI organisation in years, and hundreds of recorded rights violations: 6 right-to-life cases (3 hate-motivated killings), 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, 313 deprivations of liberty with 299 detention decisions, and expression violations rising from 216 to 540.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025) on Türkiye's leaked draft 11th Judicial Package: amendments would criminalise conduct 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' under penal-code article 225 (up to 3 years), raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care to 25, expose trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists to charges, and penalise same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to 4 years); the package rides the 'Year of the Family' framing.

Turkey permits transgender people to change their legal gender since 1988 (with surgery and court approval) but has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are unavailable, and because marriage eligibility is determined by the gender recorded in the civil registry rather than by trans status, a person who has legally changed registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender. When the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026, provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people were removed from the bill, making only symbolic same-sex weddings possible with no legal marital status. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in Istanbul and other cities in most years, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions against those who attempt to assemble — the framework under which any visible LGBT assembly in Tokat province would be policed.

HRW's World Report 2025 (covering 2024) records that the government and religious-conservative opposition parties regularly use discriminatory speech amounting to hate speech against LGBT communities on the pretext of promoting family values, which has put LGBT people at great risk. Istanbul Pride was banned for the tenth consecutive year and many cities across the country impose similar bans, so provincial authorities and police in Tokat operate within a nationwide pattern in which visible LGBT assembly is routinely banned and policed.

records.name: Trabzon
records.current_summary: No trans-specific statute, enforcement pattern or incident documentation exists for this province. The absence is recorded as absence of documented divergence, not local safety: the nationwide framework applies here in full.  As documented nationally: an October 2025 draft judicial package would criminalise conduct judged contrary to biological sex or general morality (up to three years) and same-sex ceremonies (up to four), push gender-affirming care beyond age 25 behind infertility assessments, and expose patients and providers to prosecution — protested by civic groups and the medical association. The national LGBTI monitor's 2025 report describes hostility as explicit state policy: public-institution 'family' directives, a first organisational closure in years, 3 hate-motivated killings, 89 ill-treatment violations and 299 detention decisions. And in July 2025 police mounted mass identity-check roundups in which trans women were detained and their names and images recorded without any stated legal basis — 'profiling', the detainees called it.

sources.claim: National-framework source (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): HRW, 29 Oct 2025, reports a leaked omnibus reform draft ("11th Judicial Package") that would amend the Turkish penal code to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years in prison and participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with up to four; it would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, mandate permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals, and expose both healthcare professionals performing such care and patients to criminal prosecution, with pretrial detention possible. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft; HRW calls for its withdrawal.

National-framework monitoring report (applies country-wide; no provincial breakdown): Kaos GL's Human Rights Report 2025, titled "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds LGBTI+ hostility became explicit state policy, with instructions issued to public institutions under the "Year of the Family" banner. It documents 6 right-to-life violations including 3 hate-motivated killings with trans people the most affected, 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (a striking increase over the prior year), 313 right-to-liberty violations - about 2.5 times the previous year - with 299 detention decisions, freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540, and 40 right-to-association violations including the first closure of an LGBTI+ association in many years.
